title: Design video streaming
dek: Zotato Recipes lets chefs upload short cooking videos, and 50 lakh people a day watch them on their phones, many on patchy 4G. Get a 10-minute upload ready to watch within minutes, start playback in a couple of seconds, and keep it playing in a lift.

items: Chefs upload videos of 1 to 10 minutes from their phones; they're ready to watch within a few minutes.
Viewers start playback within about 2 seconds, and the video adapts to their network instead of stalling.
Show a thumbnail and the duration; count views.
Out of scope here: live streaming (see the IND vs PAK challenge), comments, and recommendations.

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: First frame within about 2 seconds on 4G
Stalls rare; quality drops before the picture does
An upload watchable within a few minutes
5,000 uploads and 50 lakh views a day, most of them at dinner time

items: Uploads: 5,000 a day at about 300 MB each is 1.5 TB of originals a day.
Encoded sizes: all five sizes together are often smaller than a phone's original, say another 1 TB a day. Storage grows by about 2.5 TB a day; old originals can move to cheaper storage.
Viewing: 50 lakh views × about 3 minutes watched × about 1.5 Mbps is about 170 TB a day of video sent.
That's about 16 Gbps on average and around 45 Gbps at dinner. No ordinary set of servers should carry that; a CDN does.
Segments: a 5-minute video in 4-second segments is 75 segments per size, 375 files in all, each small enough to cache well.
Video: `id`, `chef_id`, `title`, `status` (uploading, processing, ready, failed, blocked), `duration`, `thumbnail`, `renditions` (the sizes available).
Rendition: `video_id`, `size` (240p…1080p), `bitrate`, `playlist_url`.
Upload: `id`, `video_id`, `parts_done`, so a dropped upload resumes where it stopped.

body.label: API
body.say: Create a video and get a signed upload address for each part. Upload the parts (a dropped part is resent alone). Say it's done. Later, get the playlist address the player opens.

body.cap: The chef's app uploads the original straight to storage. A queue hands it to transcoders that encode every chunk in five sizes in parallel. The segments and playlist are served to viewers through a CDN.

body.x: Three separate jobs: getting bytes in (storage does it), turning them into watchable pieces (the pipeline, in the background), and getting pieces out (the CDN). Your own API only handles small requests about videos, never the video itself.

body.name: First try
body.kind: ONE MACHINE ENCODES THE WHOLE VIDEO
body.what: A worker takes the upload and encodes it into each size, one after another.
body.use: Simple, and fine for short clips.
body.avoid: A 10-minute video in five sizes takes the worker 10 minutes or more. At dinner, when chefs upload most, the queue grows and videos take an hour to appear.
body.ex: A chef uploads a biryani recipe at 7 pm; it's watchable after the dinner rush is over.
body.like: One cook making every dish of a thali alone, one after the other.

body.name: Better
body.what: Cut the original into chunks of about 30 seconds (a whole number of 4-second segments) at keyframes. Every size puts keyframes at the same fixed times, so segments line up across sizes and the player can switch at any segment boundary. Each chunk and size is its own small task on any free worker. When all are done, join them in order, write the playlists and mark the video ready.
body.use: A 10-minute video becomes 20 chunks × 5 sizes = 100 small tasks; with enough workers it's ready in a minute or two.
body.avoid: Many small tasks need tracking: a task can fail or run twice, so name each output by video, chunk and size, so a rerun just overwrites the same file.
body.ex: The biryani video is split into 20 chunks at 7:00; by 7:02 every size is ready.
body.like: A kitchen line where each cook makes one part of every thali at once.

body.cap: The player picks a size for each 4-second segment from how fast the last ones downloaded. In a lift it drops to 240p for two segments and keeps playing, then climbs back to 720p.

items: The master playlist lists the sizes; each size's playlist lists its segments. The player downloads segments a few ahead of what's playing (its buffer).
Start with a small size so the first frame appears fast, then step up once the network proves quick enough.
If the buffer runs low, drop to a smaller size for the next segment. A blurry few seconds beat a spinning wheel.
Segments are standard (HLS or DASH), so phones, browsers and smart TVs all play them without special code.
Segments never change once written, so the CDN can cache them for days. Name them with the video and size, plus a version if you ever re-encode, so nothing needs to be cleared.
Popular videos are served almost entirely from the edge. Old, rarely watched videos come from your storage, and that's fine: they're few.
When a video is suddenly shared widely, its first segments are what everyone asks for; those are cached at the edge within the first few views.
An upload drops at 80%: the app resumes from the last part that arrived, not from the start.
A transcoding task fails: it's retried; after a few failures the video is marked failed and the chef is asked to upload again. Never publish a video missing a size or a chunk.
A video breaks the rules: check it (automatically, then by a person if flagged) before it's marked ready, and take it down later by marking it blocked.
Junior / mid: upload to storage, transcode to a few sizes, serve through a CDN, a player that streams.
Senior: resumable direct uploads, segments and playlists, adaptive bitrate, the bandwidth numbers and why the CDN matters.
Lead: parallel chunked encoding with safe reruns, start-up time, caching immutable segments, checks before publishing.
"Count views without slowing playback?" The player sends a small event after a few seconds of watching; count them like the ad clicks question.
"Save storage for old videos?" Keep the sizes people watch; drop rarely used ones and the original after some months, or move them to colder storage.
"Captions in Hindi and Tamil?" Separate caption files listed in the playlist; the player picks one.
"Stop people downloading the videos?" Signed segment addresses that expire make casual copying harder; real protection needs encryption with keys (DRM), which most recipe videos don't need.
"How do you test it?" Play videos through a network simulator that drops to 2G and back, and measure start time, stalls and how often quality changes.

body.x: Video lives or dies by the CDN. The IND vs PAK problem is the live version of the same idea.
body.go: Try the IND vs PAK problem

practice.brief: Each test sends what players do: fetch video segments (about 500 KB each, the same popular videos again and again), read a video's details and playlist, and now and then a chef uploads a video: its parts go straight to storage, and it is transcoded into every quality within half an hour.

tests.name: Play the next segment
tests.desc: The player asks for segment 42 of video v1 in 720p.

tests.name: Open video v1
tests.desc: The player reads v1's title, status and length.

tests.name: Upload a part
tests.desc: The chef's app sends part 3 of a new video straight to object storage with a signed link.

tests.name: Chef c1's videos
tests.desc: The newest 20 of c1's videos, newest first.

tests.name: Publish a video
tests.desc: The chef publishes video v9: it is recorded at once and transcoded after.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 8,000 requests a second: video segments and video pages.

tests.name: A viral recipe
tests.desc: At 8:10 pm a chef's 10-minute biryani video goes viral: segment requests quadruple for 15 minutes.

tests.name: A zone goes dark
tests.desc: At 8:10 pm one availability zone is lost for 15 minutes. Things may slow down, and new videos may take up to 10 minutes to be ready; nothing may be lost.

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (8,000 a second), storage and data transfer included: video's bill is mostly bandwidth. Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails.

wrong.name: Segments in the database
wrong.why: Video segments go into the rows of a table: a database is not built for big files.

wrong.name: No CDN
wrong.why: Every segment comes from object storage: when a video goes viral, it gets more requests a second than it takes.

wrong.name: Transcoding while you wait
wrong.why: The API transcodes the video before answering: publishing takes minutes and the API servers run out.

wrong.name: One zone
wrong.why: Every API server is in one zone: when it goes dark, videos don't open.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: The database has no standby: when it crashes, videos can't be opened for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: It passes every test, at a bill well above what it needs.

mutantsAllowedWhy.remove:lb: The CDN may reach the API group directly in this model.
mutantsAllowedWhy.ttl:cache: How long video details stay cached only changes how soon a new title shows; no test asks for that.
mutantsAllowedWhy.engine:db:dynamodb: DynamoDB is an equally good store for video details keyed by video.
mutantsAllowedWhy.engine:db:mongodb: MongoDB is an equally good store for video details keyed by video.

fr.label: Start playback fast and adapt to the network

api.label: Create a video (get upload part URLs)

decisions.q: Why cut videos into short segments (HLS or DASH)?
options: Short files take less disk space than one long file does
Players switch quality per segment; CDNs cache each
Segments upload faster than one long file
decisions.why: Short segments let the player pick the next one at a quality that fits the connection right now, and each one is a small file a CDN can cache. They don't save disk, and uploads are chunked separately anyway.

decisions.q: When are the different qualities made?
options: On the fly, adapted to each viewer's network as they watch
On the chef's phone before the upload, in every size
Once after upload, by transcoders taking work from a queue
decisions.why: Transcoding is slow and heavy. Doing it once per video, in the background, means every viewer gets ready-made files; doing it per viewer repeats the work lakhs of times, and phones are slow and drain their battery.

decisions.q: A phone loses its network halfway through uploading a 2 GB video. Then?
options: The upload resumes from the last part it sent
The upload starts again from the beginning
The video is kept at whatever length arrived
decisions.why: Resumable uploads in parts mean a dropped connection costs one part, not the whole file.

hints.x: Uploading, processing, watching. Which one sets the bandwidth bill?
Views × minutes × bitrate gives terabytes a day. Divide by seconds for Gbps.
Create a video and get signed URLs for each part; mark it uploaded; players fetch a playlist and then segments.
Segments never change once encoded. A CDN answers 98% of playback; your servers see 2%.
A viral video quadruples segment requests, but with the CDN in front object storage and your servers barely notice.
Behind the CDN: API servers in more than one zone, a cache for video details, a Multi-AZ database, and transcoders behind a queue.
